'''''Elymus repens''''', commonly known as '''couch grass''' {{IPAc-en|k|uː|tʃ}}, is a very common [[perennial]] species of [[Poaceae|grass]] native to most of [[Europe]], [[Asia]], the [[Arctic]], and northwest [[Africa]]. It has been brought into other mild northern climates for forage or erosion control, but it often becomes invasive in the area.

Elymus repens isn't just called '''common couch''',<ref name=BSBI07>{{BSBI 2007 |access-date=2014-10-17 }}</ref> it's also known as '''twitch''', '''quick grass''', '''quitch grass''' (also just '''quitch'''), '''dog grass''', '''quackgrass''', '''scutch grass''', and '''witchgrass'''.<ref name=grin>{{GRIN | ''Elymus repens'' subsp. ''repens'' | 454279 | access-date = 2017-12-15}}</ref><ref name=fnwe>Flora of NW Europe: {{Deprecated archive|url=https://archive.today/20070621080912/http://ip30.eti.uva.nl/BIS/flora.php?selected=beschrijving&menuentry=soorten&id=4625|title=''Elytrigia repens''}}</ref><ref name=foc>Flora of China: [http://www.efloras.org/florataxon.aspx?flora_id=2&taxon_id=200025323 ''Elytrigia repens'']</ref><ref>Webster Third International Dictionary (Könemann, 1993) {{ISBN|3-8290-5292-8}}</ref>

==Description==
It has creeping [[rhizome]]s which enable it to grow rapidly across [[grassland]]. It has flat, hairy leaves with upright flower spikes. The stems ([[Culm (botany)|'culms']]) grow to {{ Convert | 40–150 | cm }} tall; the [[leaf|leaves]] are linear, {{ Convert | 15–40 | cm }} long and {{ Convert | 3–10 | mm }} broad at the base of the plant, with leaves higher on the stems {{ Convert | 2–8.5 | mm }} broad. The [[flower]] spike is {{ Convert | 10–30 | mm }} long, with spikelets {{ Convert | 1–2 | cm }} long, {{ Convert | 5–7 | mm }} broad and {{ Convert | 3 | mm }} thick with three to eight florets. The [[glume]]s are {{ Convert | 7–12 | mm }} long, usually without an [[awn (botany)|awn]] or with only a short one.

It flowers at the end of June through to August in the Northern Hemisphere.<ref name=fnwe/><ref name=foc/><ref name=fitter>Fitter, R., Fitter, A., & Farrer, A. (1984). ''Collins Guide to the Grasses, Sedges, Rushes and Ferns of Britain and Northern Europe''. Collins {{ISBN|0-00-219128-8}}.</ref><ref>Hubbard, C. E. ''Grasses''. Penguin Books, 1978</ref>

==Taxonomy==
{{self-contradictory|article|date=January 2026}}
Various taxonomic subdivisions of this species have been proposed. Moreover, it is assigned to various genera (''Elymus'', ''Elytrigium'', ''Agropyron''). In a recent classification, three [[subspecies]] are distinguished, one of these with an additional [[variety (biology)|variety]]:<ref name=grin/><ref name=fnwe/><ref name=foc/>
*''Elytrigia repens'' subsp. ''repens''. Throughout most of the range of the species.
**''Elytrigia repens'' subsp. ''repens'' var. ''repens''. Awns usually absent or if present, very short.
**''Elytrigia repens'' subsp. ''repens'' var. ''aristata'' (Döll) P.D.Sell. Awns present, up to 15 mm long.
*''Elytrigia repens'' subsp. ''elongatiformis'' (Drobow) Tzvelev (syn. ''Elytrigia elongatiformis'' (Drobow) Nevski). Central and southwestern Asia, far southeastern Europe (Ukraine).
*''Elytrigia repens'' subsp. ''longearistata'' N. R. Cui. Western China (Xinjiang).

[[Hybrid (biology)|Hybrids]] are recorded with several related grasses, including ''[[Elytrigia juncea]]'' (''Elytrigia × laxa'' (Fr.) Kerguélen), ''[[Elytrigia atherica]]'' (''Elytrigia × drucei'' Stace), and with the [[barley]] species ''[[Hordeum secalinum]]'' (''× Elytrordeum langei'' (K. Richt.) Hyl.).<ref name=fnwe/>

==Ecology==
The foliage is an important forage grass for many grazing [[mammal]]s.<ref name=foc/> The [[seed]]s are eaten by several species of grassland [[bird]]s, particularly [[Emberiza|buntings]] and [[finch]]es.<ref name=bwpc>Snow, D. W. & Perrins, C. M. (1998). ''The Birds of the Western Palearctic'' Concise Edition. OUP {{ISBN|0-19-854099-X}}.</ref> The [[caterpillar]]s of some [[Lepidoptera]] use it as a foodplant, e.g. the [[Essex skipper]] (''Thymelicus lineola'').

==Eradication==
Couch grass has become [[naturalisation (biology)|naturalised]] throughout much of the world, and is often listed as an [[invasive plant|invasive weed]].<ref name=grin/> It is very difficult to remove from garden environments, as the thin rhizomes become entangled among the roots of shrubs and perennials, and each severed piece of [[rhizome]] can develop into a new plant. It may be possible to loosen the earth around the plant, and carefully pull out the complete rhizome. 
This is best done in the spring, when disturbed plants can recover.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://apps.rhs.org.uk/advicesearch/profile.aspx?PID=283 |title=Couch grass / Royal Horticultural Society |publisher=Apps.rhs.org.uk |date=2012-02-27 |access-date=2012-10-13 |archive-date=2012-10-07 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20121007032740/http://apps.rhs.org.uk/advicesearch/Profile.aspx?pid=283 |url-status=dead }}</ref><ref name=Hessayon>{{cite book|last=Hessayon|first=Dr D. G.|author-link = D. G. Hessayon|title=The pest & weed expert|year=2007|publisher=Expert|location=United Kingdom|isbn=978-0903505628|page=128}}</ref>  Another method is to dig deep into the ground in order to remove as much of the grass as possible. The area should then be covered with a thick layer of woodchips. To further prevent re-growth, cardboard can be placed underneath the woodchips. The long, white rhizomes will, however, dry out and die if left on the surface. Many herbicides will also control it.

==Applications==
